title: Sunnah and hadith
hook: the sunnah is his way; hadith are the reports that carry it

segments.voice: Yesterday: the hadith, a report of what the Prophet said, did, or approved.

A twig. A short stick from the arak tree, chewed at one end until it frays into a brush. It's called a miswak, and in mosques today you can still see someone pull one from a pocket before prayer. Why carry a twig? Because of a sentence in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said that if it would not be too hard on his community, he would have ordered them to use the miswak before every prayer. He didn't order it. He used it himself. So people still do. Today, sunnah and hadith.
screen: `A TWIG FROM THE ARAK TREE.` → `HE WOULD HAVE ORDERED IT.` → `HE DIDN'T. HE USED IT.`

segments.voice: You met the word sunnah long ago, in what the Prophet left behind. Sunnah is usually put into English as a way, a path, a habit of life. The Sunnah, capital S, is the way of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: how he prayed, ate, spoke, forgave, traded, slept. Hadith are the reports. The sunnah is the way; hadith are how the way reaches people who never saw him. Why it matters: the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much." An example is something you watch. Hadith let later people watch. Not everything travels by written report alone. In Bukhari, the Prophet tells his companions: pray as you have seen me praying. The prayer was carried by people standing beside people, generation after generation. The Maliki school gives real weight to the living practice of Medina, the city where he lived and died. Shia scholarship looks to the Imams of his family as trusted carriers and teachers of his way. Each, in its own terms, asks: how does his way reach us? One more thing: the word does two jobs. In the law, sunnah also names a recommended act, rewarded but not required, like the sunnah prayers around the obligatory ones, or the miswak. So "it's sunnah" can mean it's his way, or that it's recommended; context tells you which. Aisha reports, in Bukhari, that he liked to begin with the right: putting on his sandals, combing his hair, washing for prayer, and in all his affairs.
screen: `THE WAY, AND THE REPORTS.` · `A GOOD EXAMPLE TO WATCH.` · `PRAY AS YOU'VE SEEN ME PRAY.` · `A RECOMMENDED ACT, TOO.`

segments.voice: Pick one small sunnah from these reports: beginning with the right as you put on your shoes, cleaning your teeth with care before a prayer or a conversation that matters, or helping with the work at home before you leave it. If you're not Muslim, you can still try one to understand how Muslims live it, the way you'd try a recipe from a friend's grandmother.
Sunnah and hadith. The sunnah is the Prophet's way of life; hadith are the reports that carry it. Today's word.
Your line: the way, carried. Handed from person to person. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the sunnah from hadith, from teachers and from family practice, and keep small daily sunnahs such as starting with the right, using the miswak and praying the recommended sunnah prayers.

chat.says: When people say something is 'sunnah', what do they actually mean?
options: It can mean the Prophet's way, or a recommended act. Context tells you which.
It always means an act that's strictly required, like the five daily prayers.
It means an old Arabian custom, unrelated to the Prophet's own life.
